audience.programmeDescription: Marine Sciences studies oceans, seas and coasts as linked ecological, physical and social systems. WUR combines marine biology and food systems with climate, economics, governance, spatial methods and the design of sustainable solutions.
audience.comparisonExplanation: These UCR programmes approach marine and coastal questions through different combinations of biology, environmental science, data, economics and governance. WUR offers a more extensive specialist marine sequence, including dedicated field courses, aquatic-animal and aquaculture study, ocean processes and a required marine thesis. UCR’s optional independent research is additional to the illustrated 180 credits; a marine project is not guaranteed.

componentNotes.bms-choice: Three-credit restricted choice between Mathematics Applied: Introduction and Statistics 1. This example takes the first-listed Mathematics Applied: Introduction, for a student with Mathematics A preparation; it precedes Mathematics Applied: Analysis. Statistics 2 assumes active high-school statistics or Statistics 1.
componentNotes.bms-thesis: Required 12-credit individual research thesis, with a proposal, research, report, presentation and defence. Entry requires at least 102 programme credits, all 60 first-year credits and Research Methods for Marine Sciences; the coordinator checks preparation with the study adviser. The boundary-crossing and personal-leadership portfolio must also pass. Assessment covers research execution (40%), the report (40%), presentation (10%) and defence (10%).
componentNotes.bms-leadership: The 3-credit course includes a core and a learning ribbon across six required courses, ending during the thesis. Passing its portfolio is required for the thesis grade; these are not extra credits.
componentNotes.bms-field-project: Integrated marine field research includes intertidal sampling, sediment transport, fish ecology and observations of Wadden Sea uses. Laboratory and fieldwork safety are required; BMS students have admission priority.
componentNotes.bms-marine-methods: Research design, marine sampling and monitoring, data analysis and a multi-day overseas field practical. Laboratory and fieldwork safety are required.
componentNotes.bms-electives: Thirty open credits can be used for a minor and/or individual electives. No particular minor, placement or specialist package is assumed.

programmeTitles: Coastal climate, spatial evidence & sustainable systems
concepts: Combines marine ecology and biological foundations with water and chemical processes, geospatial research, food-system sustainability, economics, law and environmental governance. It connects ecological evidence with decisions about coastal environments and marine resources.

Prioritises the ecological and biological mechanisms of marine biodiversity and conservation, supported by evolution, molecular and biochemical foundations, laboratory skills and quantitative environmental investigation.

Prioritises climate effects, coastal water, nature-based interventions and spatial and data evidence, with environmental and energy-system appraisal. Marine ecology provides the ecological setting; energy study does not reproduce offshore engineering.

notes.text: WUR combines marine and coastal field research, aquatic-animal biology, aquaculture, ocean processes, marine governance and a required marine thesis. UCR offers a related combination of marine biology, ecology, environmental science, spatial/data methods and governance. It does not reproduce WUR’s full specialist marine sequence, dedicated field methods or aquaculture training.

comparisonAlignment: Shared evolutionary genetics, variation, selection and adaptation form a direct substantive relationship; the scope and credit weights differ.
Shared population/community ecology, food webs and ecosystem processes provide a direct ecological foundation.
Shared marine and estuarine organisms, habitats, ecological processes and human pressures; WUR additionally includes specific field practicals and excursions.

Both examine environmental effects and sustainability of biological food-production systems, including aquaculture. UCR is predominantly comparative farming; WUR integrates seafood supply, trade and governance.
Both substantively address molecular/cellular organisation, membranes, signalling and regulation. WUR includes its own laboratory applications.

The selected general biodiversity survey does not adequately reproduce this dedicated marine-organism adaptation, dissection and intertidal-field component. The strongest marine course already represents Marine Ecology; preserve this distinct specialist gap.

Shared water/compound chemistry, carbonate and nutrient/contaminant processes support part of the flows-and-cycles component. Ocean currents, tides, sediment transport and integrated marine socio-economics are additional WUR scope.
Both develop nature-based coastal/water interventions that combine ecosystem function with human goals; WUR uses a dedicated marine evaluation/design framework and design pitch.

Shared appraisal of coastal/delta water responses, ecological effects and trade-offs directly addresses part of nature-based-solution assessment. WUR adds modelled scenarios and integrated ecosystem-service reports.
Shared climate impacts, sea-level rise and adaptation/mitigation connect climate to water and marine systems; WUR adds explicit hydrological flows and a marine-case systems analysis.
Market failure, externalities, public goods and policy appraisal are substantive shared economic tools. WUR applies resource-economics concepts to fisheries, conservation and competing ocean uses.
Shared legal systems, legal reasoning and case-law analysis provide a meaningful introductory law relationship; WUR focuses on rules and scientific evidence for life/marine sciences.
Both directly analyse institutions, resource users, participation and policy at multiple scales. WUR dedicates the component to ocean/coastal governance.
Spatial evidence, research, modelling & open study
Shared inference, hypothesis tests and regression are specific statistical content, with different mathematical depth and applications.
Shared research design and qualitative sampling/interview/observation methods support human-environment inquiry. WUR specifically develops a complete research proposal and combines strategies.
Shared differentiation, integration and differential equations provide direct mathematical content; the UCR course includes additional modelling and computational work.

Shared statistical model fitting, classification, validation and data-science analysis address a specific part of WUR modelling. UCR does not reproduce coupled ecosystem, economic and spatial simulation.
Shared geospatial data, projections, queries, transformations, terrain/surface analysis and remote sensing provide a direct GIS relationship.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Econometrics
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
